howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET
tips: Voltage (V_DS): leave real margin above the highest voltage in the circuit, including spikes.
Current (I_D): the headline rating is usually at 25°C case temperature. Derate for your real operating temperature.
R_DS(on): lower means less heat, but R_DS(on) rises as the junction heats up.
Gate drive: logic-level types turn on fully at 4.5 V or lower; standard types need about 10 V.
Package: TO-220 and TO-247 suit heatsinks; TO-252 and SO-8 rely on PCB copper; SOT-23 is for small loads.
Channel: N-channel for low-side switching; P-channel for high-side switching and reverse-polarity protection.

mosfetCalculator.h2: MOSFET Thermal and Power Loss Calculator
mosfetCalculator.workedExample: Worked Example: IRFZ44N, I_RMS 10 A, R_DS(on) 17.5 mΩ, T_A 40°C, θ_JA 62°C/W. Conduction loss P_cond = 1.75 W. Temperature rise = 108.5°C. T_J = 148.5°C, just under the limit. If R_DS(on) rises to ~30 mΩ when hot, loss becomes 3 W and T_J reaches ~226°C, which fails. That is why designers add a heatsink or pick a lower-resistance part.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for Hot, Dusty, High-Ambient Conditions
tips: Derate generously: a MOSFET in a 50°C enclosure has far less thermal headroom than the datasheet's 25°C figures suggest.

Think about dust: sealed enclosures trap heat, so plan airflow or conduction cooling.
Surge and lightning: long cable runs pick up spikes, so add TVS diodes and gate protection.
Parallel carefully: use matched parts, equal gate resistors and a symmetrical layout.

Parallel carefully: use matched parts, equal gate resistors and a symmetrical layout.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for Lighting Drivers and Power Supplies
tips: Voltage: A 230V supply rectifies to about 325V DC, and spikes sit on top, so 500V or 600V parts are common. Don't run a part close to its rating.
R_DS(on): High-voltage MOSFETs have high on-resistance, so they heat up even at modest current.
Switching loss: At higher frequencies, switching loss and gate charge matter as much as conduction loss.
Heat in enclosures: Sealed LED drivers trap heat, so derate and consider the case temperature.
Spikes: Transformers and inductors produce voltage spikes, so add snubbers and TVS diodes.
Inrush and surge: Lighting loads see inrush at switch-on, and fluctuating grid supply stresses the input stage, so protect the input.

mosfetCalculator.h2: MOSFET Thermal and Power Loss Calculator

workedExample.note: STP10NK60Z in an LED driver. R_DS(on) 0.75 Ω (750 mΩ), T_A 35°C, θ_JA 62°C/W (TO-220, free air). At 1 A: P_cond = 1 x 1 x 0.75 = 0.75 W. Temp rise = 46.5°C. T_J = 81.5°C (Safe). At 1.5 A: P_cond = 1.69 W. Temp rise = 104.6°C. T_J = 139.6°C (Warning).

mosfetCalculator.disclaimer: Disclaimer: this is a quick estimate. Real designs also include switching loss, duty cycle, PCB cooling and the rise of R_DS(on) with temperature. Check the datasheet. R_DS(on) is quoted at 25°C and rises considerably when the junction is hot.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for 24V Vehicle and Industrial DC Systems
tips: Voltage: A nominal 24V system can see much higher voltage during charging and load-dump events, so 60V to 100V parts are common, and higher-voltage DC buses need 150V or 200V.
Inductive loads: Solenoids and motors need a flyback diode or TVS, or the MOSFET will fail from the inductive spike.
Reverse polarity: Batteries get connected the wrong way, so a P-channel MOSFET or a series diode protects the circuit.
Heat in enclosures: Panels and vehicle boxes trap heat, so derate and use a heatsink.
Gate drive: Logic-level parts suit 5V controllers, and standard parts need about 10 V. Add a gate resistor and a pull-down.
Vibration and connectors: Vehicle and rail equipment shakes, so choose reliable connectors and locking terminals as well as the right MOSFET.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for Furnace, Servo and Solenoid Stages
tips: Voltage: Motor and solenoid loads kick back inductive spikes, so leave real margin above the DC bus and add a flyback diode, TVS or snubber.
Heat: Foundry floors are hot, so derate generously and use a real heatsink with a good thermal pad.
Gate drive: Make sure the driver supplies enough gate voltage and current, and add a gate resistor. Weak drive adds switching loss.
Short circuits: Furnaces and welders see fault conditions, so protect the gate and consider current sensing.
Find the cause of a failure: When replacing a failed MOSFET, check the gate driver, snubber and supply, or the new part will fail too.
Parallel carefully: Use matched parts, equal gate resistors and a symmetrical layout.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for Marine and Humid-Coastal Use
tips: Voltage: Batteries charge above their nominal voltage, and alternators and inductive loads add spikes, so a 12V system commonly uses 40V to 60V parts and a 24V system 60V to 100V.
Reverse polarity: Batteries get connected the wrong way, so a P-channel MOSFET or a series diode protects the circuit.
Corrosion: Salt air eats exposed leads, connectors and boards, so use conformal coating, sealed enclosures, quality connectors and terminal blocks.
Heat in sealed boxes: Sealed enclosures trap heat, so derate and use a real heatsink.
Gate drive: Logic-level parts suit 5V controllers, and standard parts need about 10 V. Add a gate resistor and a pull-down.
Find the cause of a failure: When replacing a failed MOSFET, check for moisture damage, corroded connectors and a faulty gate driver, or the new part will fail too.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for Solar Inverters and Charge Controllers
tips: Voltage: A solar array's open-circuit voltage is higher than its operating voltage, and cold mornings raise it further, so leave real margin above the highest voltage the panel can reach.
Battery side: 12V, 24V and 48V batteries charge above their nominal voltage, and inductive spikes add more, so 40V to 100V parts are common.
Derate for heat: Karnataka's plateau summers and sealed enclosures eat into thermal headroom, so use a real heatsink and good airflow.
Gate drive: Make sure the driver supplies enough gate voltage and current, and add a gate resistor. Slow switching adds heat.
Surge and lightning: Long panel and pump cables pick up spikes, so add TVS diodes and gate protection.
Parallel carefully: Use matched parts, equal gate resistors and a symmetrical layout.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for an EV or Drone Controller
tips: Voltage: A 48V pack can reach about 54V when charged, and regeneration and switching spikes add more, so 100V parts are common for 48V systems.
Current: Package-limited ratings are lower than silicon ratings, and the headline figure is at 25°C case temperature, so derate it.
R_DS(on): Lower resistance means less heat, but gate charge rises, so a slower driver adds switching loss.
Gate drive: Use a proper driver with enough peak current, plus a gate resistor and a pull-down.
Layout: Keep power loops short, because stray inductance causes voltage spikes.
Parallel carefully: Use matched parts, equal gate resistors and a symmetrical layout.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for Inverters, Pumps and Humid Conditions
tips: Voltage: Batteries charge above their nominal voltage, and pump motors kick back inductive spikes, so a 12V system commonly uses 40V to 60V parts and a 24V or 48V system 60V to 150V.
Moisture: Monsoon humidity corrodes leads, connectors and boards, so use conformal coating, sealed enclosures, quality connectors and terminal blocks, and check for corrosion on every repair.
Heat in sealed boxes: Sealed enclosures trap heat, so derate and use a real heatsink.
Gate drive: Make sure the driver supplies enough gate voltage and current, and add a gate resistor and a pull-down.
Surge and lightning: Malnad thunderstorms and long cable runs to pumps pick up spikes, so add TVS diodes and gate protection.
Find the cause of a failure: When replacing a failed MOSFET, check for moisture damage, corroded connectors and a faulty gate driver, or the new part will fail too.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for Extreme Heat and Dust
tips: Derate hard: With ambient temperatures that can reach the mid-40s °C, and higher inside a sealed panel, a MOSFET has far less thermal headroom than the datasheet's 25°C figures suggest. Choose a part with more margin than you think you need.
Heatsink properly: Use a real heatsink, a good thermal pad and clear airflow, and clean dust off regularly.
Voltage: Motor loads kick back inductive spikes, so leave real margin above the DC bus. A rectified 230V supply gives about 325V DC, so 500V and 600V parts are common on the mains side.
Gate drive: Make sure the driver supplies enough gate voltage and current, and add a gate resistor.
Surge protection: Long cable runs to pumps and solar arrays pick up spikes, so add TVS diodes.
Find the cause of a failure: When replacing a failed MOSFET, check the gate driver, cooling and supply, or the new part will fail too.

tips: Voltage: a 230V supply rectifies to about 325V DC, and spikes sit on top, so 500V to 650V parts are common on the mains side. Battery-side stages use 40V to 100V parts, with margin for charging voltage and spikes.
R_DS(on): high-voltage MOSFETs have high on-resistance, so they heat up even at modest current.
Switching loss: at higher frequencies, gate charge and switching loss matter as much as conduction loss.
Heat in enclosures: sealed drivers and rooftop inverter boxes trap heat, and Gujarat summers are hot, so derate and use a real heatsink.
Spikes and surges: transformers, long panel cables and grid fluctuations produce spikes, so add snubbers and TVS diodes.
Find the cause of a failure: when replacing a failed MOSFET, check the gate driver, snubber, supply and cooling, or the new part will fail too.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for Servo, Stepper and BLDC Machine Drives
tips: Voltage: motors kick back inductive spikes and regenerate onto the bus, so leave real margin above the supply. A 48V bus commonly uses 100V parts, and a 24V bus 60V parts.
Current and temperature: the headline current is quoted at 25°C case temperature. Polishing and embroidery machines run for long shifts in warm rooms, so derate for continuous operation.
R_DS(on) and gate charge: lower resistance means less heat, but a bigger gate charge slows switching, so match the gate driver to the part.
Gate drive: make sure the driver supplies enough peak current, and add a gate resistor and pull-down.
Layout: keep power loops short, because stray inductance makes voltage spikes that kill MOSFETs.
Find the cause of a failure: when replacing a failed MOSFET in a drive, check the gate driver, the motor winding and the supply, or the new part will fail too.

Temperature rise = 40.5°C. T_J = 80.5°C (Safe). At 30 A: P_cond = 30 x 30 x 0.0045 = 4.05 W. Temperature rise = 162°C. T_J = 202°C (Warning). This shows how heat grows with the square of the current, so doubling the current quadruples the loss. A heatsink lowers the thermal resistance and gives real margin.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for DC Systems and Plant Drives
tips: Voltage: a 110V DC battery system charges to well above its nominal voltage, and switching adds spikes, so 150V to 250V parts are common. A rectified 230V supply gives about 325V DC, so 500V parts are common on the mains side.

howToPick.title: How to Pick a MOSFET for Mill Drives, Presses and Kiln-Side Panels
tips: Voltage: motor loads kick back inductive spikes, so leave real margin above the DC bus. A rectified 230V supply gives about 325V DC, and a 415V three-phase supply gives about 560V DC, so 600V and higher parts are common in drive stages.
Heat: kiln halls and plant panels are very hot, so derate generously and use a real heatsink with a good thermal pad.
Dust: fine ceramic dust is abrasive and clogs heatsinks and fans, so use filtered, sealed enclosures and clean airflow paths regularly.
Gate drive: make sure the driver supplies enough gate voltage and current, and add a gate resistor and a pull-down.
Surge protection: long cable runs and heavy switching loads produce spikes, so add TVS diodes and snubbers.
Find the cause of a failure: when replacing a failed MOSFET in a drive, check the gate driver, snubber, supply, motor and cooling, or the new part will fail too.

mosfetCalculator.h2: MOSFET Thermal and Power Loss Calculator

At 3 A: P_cond = 3 x 3 x 0.18 = 1.62 W. Temperature rise = 64.8°C. T_J = 109.8°C (Safe). At 5 A: P_cond = 5 x 5 x 0.18 = 4.5 W. Temperature rise = 180°C. T_J = 225°C (Warning). This shows why high-voltage MOSFETs need a heatsink even at modest currents, because their on-resistance is high and heat grows with the square of the current.

Induction heating: the stage sees high-frequency switching and resonant spikes, so match gate drive, snubbers and voltage margin to the topology.
Heat: furnace halls and plating shops are hot, so derate generously and use a real heatsink with a good thermal pad.
Corrosion: plating fumes and sea air eat leads, connectors and boards, so use conformal coating, sealed enclosures and quality terminal blocks.
Gate drive: make sure the driver supplies enough gate voltage and current, and add a gate resistor and a pull-down.
Find the cause of a failure: when replacing a failed MOSFET, check the gate driver, snubber, supply, cooling and any corrosion, or the new part will fail too.
